title: Trump Says US-Iran Talks Resume This Week via Qatar as Yemen's Army Launches a 756-Operation Push Against the Houthis and Germany Confronts a Hybrid-War Campaign
subhead: Washington and Tehran edge back toward indirect talks after Trump rejected Iran's Hormuz proposal, while Saudi-backed Yemeni forces escalate across seven fronts and Berlin weighs wartime conscription measures after 200 Russian hybrid attacks in 2026.

sections.heading: US-Iran Talks Set to Resume as Hormuz Standoff Holds
sections.body:
President Donald Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after rejecting Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. 'They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,' Trump told Axios, adding that Iranian leaders 'overplayed their hand.' Axios reported, citing sources, that indirect talks could begin as early as Monday, conducted through Qatari mediators and following earlier contacts between US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Iran is holding its line. Foreign Minister Araghchi said the Strait can be opened only through diplomatic dialogue, and Tehran insists it is still awaiting a formal US response to its proposal. Trump also claimed that more than 20 million barrels of oil transited the strait over the weekend, the largest volume since the war began. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, as fuel prices weigh on public opinion.
sections.whyItMatters: The two sides are not converging on substance, but the resumption of Qatari-mediated talks keeps a narrow diplomatic channel open even as Trump openly contemplates new strikes. Oil flows rebounding while the dispute festers means the market is pricing a pause, not a resolution.

sections.heading: Yemen: Government Forces Widen Offensive Against the Houthis
sections.body:
Yemen's internationally recognised government said its forces carried out 756 operations against Houthi positions across seven fronts in 72 hours, killing or wounding 2,316 fighters, according to a statement by armed forces spokesman Brigadier General Majeed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili carried by the Saba news agency. The military also claimed that four Iranian specialists in drone and missile operations were killed in Taiz, calling it confirmation of continued Iranian support for the Houthis. The casualty figures could not be independently verified.

The escalation centres on Taiz, where fighting has intensified around strategic highlands and the Taiz-Aden route. On Sunday a Saudi airstrike hit a market in the province, killing seven and wounding 40 according to the Houthi-run health ministry, while Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthi fighters had established a military camp near the market, leaving the target and circumstances disputed. Displacement in the province has risen to roughly 169,000, per Arab News.
sections.whyItMatters: Iranian personnel reportedly dying alongside Houthi fighters shows Tehran's proxy network remains active even while it negotiates with Washington over Hormuz. A widening Taiz campaign risks drawing Saudi Arabia deeper into a ground war it had sought to wind down.

sections.heading: Germany: Hybrid War and Conscription Reshape a Post-War Taboo
sections.body:
ABC News reported Monday that German intelligence has attributed an August plot at Leipzig Airport to Russia, describing it as a sharp escalation in Moscow's hybrid campaign against NATO states. Explosive-laden drones flew into the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov aircraft loaded with 25,000 litres of jet fuel; a soup can packed with 600 grams of Semtex was found among the debris after the payload failed to detonate. Colonel Johan Schmid, a senior German officer specialising in Russian hybrid aggression, told the ABC that Moscow has launched at least 200 hybrid attacks in 2026, a figure NATO suspects is far higher.

The pressure is driving a domestic rethink. More than 45,000 students walked out of classes across some 100 German cities and towns on Friday to protest military service reforms they fear will lead to compulsory enlistment, according to Anadolu via Kayhan. Reports also circulated that German males aged 17 to 45 now face new restrictions on travel abroad requiring military approval, a measure that would mark a significant break with the country's post-1945 constraints.
sections.whyItMatters: Germany is being pushed to reverse foundational post-WWII limits on military mobilisation in response to sustained sabotage and drone incursions on its soil. The scale of student protest shows the political cost: rearmament is colliding with a population that did not sign up for a wartime footing.

sections.heading: South China Sea: US Condemns Chinese Maneuvers at Ayungin Shoal
sections.body:
US Ambassador to Manila Lee Lipton condemned what he called 'dangerous blocking and other irresponsible maneuvers' by the China Coast Guard and People's Liberation Army Navy that threatened a collision with a Philippine vessel and prevented a resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal (Ayungin Shoal) on September 24, according to The Philippine Star. The Armed Forces of the Philippines said three Chinese Navy warships and five CCG vessels, including two Houbei-class missile boats, interfered with the humanitarian rotation and resupply of troops aboard the grounded BRP Sierra Madre.

The Philippines suspended the mission over escalation risk. Lipton called on Beijing to cease 'escalatory tactics' and affirmed US support for its treaty ally. The incident is the latest in a pattern of confrontations at the shoal, which Manila holds under the 2016 arbitral award that China rejects.
sections.whyItMatters: A blocked resupply at a Philippine outpost is a direct test of the US-Philippine mutual defence treaty. With a Trump-Xi trade truce freshly extended, the incident shows maritime flashpoints between the two powers remain live even as their economic relationship stabilises.

sections.heading: Indo-Pacific: Japan to Deploy Long-Range Missiles in US Joint Drills
sections.body:
Japan's Ground Self-Defense Force will for the first time deploy long-range attack missiles — the Type 12 — during major US-Japan joint exercises beginning in October, according to Japan Today and the Asahi Shimbun. Reports noted the systems' range covers stretches of the Chinese coast, a significant step in Japan's move toward stand-off strike capability. Separately, TASS reported that US Typhon systems will be stationed at Kadena base after drills in Japan, with the American side describing the move as non-permanent.

The deployments follow a Trump-Xi summit that ended with a two-month trade truce extension and a new AI dialogue but no breakthrough on security issues. Beijing has repeatedly criticised US missile deployments to the region.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan putting offensive-range missiles into a joint exercise marks the continued normalisation of strike capability that Tokyo long avoided. Combined with US Typhon placements, it strengthens the first-island-chain posture — and raises the risk of Chinese counter-moves.

sections.heading: Africa and Diplomacy: DRC Crash, Tigray Strike, and a Summit's Contested Accounts
sections.body:
A plane carrying a Congolese military delegation crashed in the Democratic Republic of Congo, killing 17 people including four civilians, with two senior armed forces members and the head of the High Military Court and army auditor general among the dead, according to Al Jazeera and Geo News. In Ethiopia, a drone strike hit the Tigrai TV headquarters in Mekelle, halting broadcasts, as fighting escalated in the north, per Al Bawaba and AFP. Human Rights Watch on September 25 called for an investigation into an airstrike in Tigray that wounded 13 civilians as a possible war crime.

On the diplomatic front, China and the US issued competing accounts of the Xi-Trump summit. Beijing listed eight agreed outcomes including an AI dialogue and tariff cuts on selected goods, while the White House fact sheet differed in emphasis, according to Seoul Economic Daily. CFR analysts characterised the summit as largely symbolic.
sections.whyItMatters: The rival summit readouts show that even a managed US-China detente produces contested agreements rather than a shared framework. Meanwhile, the DRC crash removes senior military and judicial figures at a moment of fragile security in the eastern Congo, and Tigray's renewed strikes signal Ethiopia's fragile 2022 peace is eroding.

bottomLine: Iran and the US are heading back to indirect talks through Qatar even as Trump rejects Tehran's Hormuz terms and muses about new strikes — a pause, not a settlement, with oil flows recovering but the underlying dispute unresolved. Yemen's government offensive and the reported deaths of Iranian specialists show Tehran's proxy network remains engaged on other fronts. In Europe, Germany is being forced to consider reversing post-1945 military limits after a year of Russian hybrid attacks, and the resulting student protests show the political price. In Asia, Japan's first long-range missile deployment in US drills and a blocked Philippine resupply mission underline that US-China rivalry persists beneath a freshly extended trade truce.
